lesson.title: When Reality Fractures: Understanding Schizophrenia
lesson.summary: Schizophrenia is a serious, chronic psychological disorder involving disturbances in thought, perception, and behavior severe enough to significantly impair functioning, classified as a psychotic disorder because it can involve a loss of contact with shared reality.
lesson.body:
Schizophrenia is one of the most serious conditions covered in the study of psychological disorders, and also one of the most misunderstood. It is a chronic psychological disorder that disrupts a person's thinking, perception, emotional expression, and behavior severely enough to significantly impair their ability to function in daily life. Under the DSM classification system, schizophrenia is classified as a psychotic disorder, meaning that, at least during active episodes, it involves some genuine loss of contact with consensus reality, not simply unusual thoughts or eccentric behavior.

Consistent with what you already know about defining psychological disorders, a diagnosis of schizophrenia is not made from a single strange experience. The DSM generally requires two or more characteristic symptoms to be present for a significant portion of time during a one month period, with some signs of disturbance persisting for at least six months overall, along with a clear decline in functioning, such as work, relationships, or self-care, compared to before the disorder's onset.

Psychologists typically organize schizophrenia's symptoms into broad categories. Positive symptoms refer to experiences added on top of ordinary functioning, things like hallucinations and delusions, that most people do not have. Negative symptoms refer to normal functions that are reduced or absent, such as flattened emotional expression, reduced motivation, and social withdrawal. Many people with schizophrenia also experience cognitive difficulties, including problems with attention, working memory, and executive function. The next two chapters go into positive and negative symptoms in much more depth.

Schizophrenia typically emerges in late adolescence through the twenties, and research has generally found a somewhat earlier average age of onset in men than in women, though there is real variability. Its course also varies considerably from person to person: some people experience a single episode with substantial recovery, while others experience a more chronic, relapsing pattern. With appropriate treatment, typically a combination of antipsychotic medication and psychosocial support such as therapy, skills training, and family or community support, many people with schizophrenia are able to manage their symptoms and lead meaningful lives. It is important to resist the pop culture tendency to treat a schizophrenia diagnosis as a tragic endpoint.

It's also worth directly correcting a very common misconception: schizophrenia does not mean a "split personality" or multiple distinct identities, that description actually applies to a separate and much rarer condition, dissociative identity disorder. The name schizophrenia comes from Greek roots meaning roughly "split mind," but the split it refers to is a splitting apart of normally connected mental functions, thought, emotion, and perception no longer working together in a typical, integrated way, not a division into separate personalities.

As with other disorders you've studied, schizophrenia's causes appear to be multifactorial, involving genetic and neurodevelopmental vulnerability interacting with environmental stressors, which is exactly the kind of picture the biological perspective on disorders would predict. One neurotransmitter system in particular, dopamine, has received enormous research attention in schizophrenia, which is the focus of the dopamine hypothesis covered later in this unit.
